SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN) -- Walt Peters knows what it's like to fear for his life. He knows how it feels to board a plane, deploying for combat. He knows the feeling of making it home alive. Walt Peters is often among the last people soldiers see as they deploy and the first they see upon their return. That's why the retired Vietnam veteran has stood outside at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, for the past four years as a beacon of pride and support, welcoming home returning soldiers and wishing "Godspeed" to those deploying. "To me, if it wasn't for our soldiers and our veterans, we would not have this beautiful country," says Peters. "These guys are our freedom." Peters, 64, has been one of the last people that about 20,000 soldiers so far have seen before boarding the plane for the war zone -- and one of the first seen upon return. No matter what time the soldiers' flights are arriving or departing -- many take place in the middle of the night -- Peters is there to shake their hands and give them a token of support: a small American flag. Some of those flags, Peters says, have gone to Iraq and back. "When they touch that flag, we're giving them a piece of our country, saying, 'Thank you.'" Peters is not the only volunteer showing his support at each flight. But he does all of this nearly blind. He says learned he had chemical diabetes nearly 10 years ago after he was exposed to Agent Orange during his Vietnam tours. He has lost almost all of his sight over the past few years, but that hasn't depleted his dedication to the soldiers. "When I went to Vietnam on my tours I'd never had this. I had never had nobody say, 'We appreciate your service. We thank you for what you're doing for our freedom,'" Peters says. "When they get on that plane, they're gonna know that this old Vietnam vet cares." Peters first became involved greeting flights through the Savannah Red Cross in 2004 when a friend from his fraternal Moose Lodge brought him to welcome a returning flight. Peters has since become a flight greeting leader, bringing in and training his own volunteers. His crew includes Moose members and Vietnam veterans. So many flights come in, Peters says, that it's impossible to be present for all of them. He's worked as many as three flights in one day, in a 26-hour period.   Watch how Peters sends off and greets deploying and returning U.S. soldiers » . Peters and his volunteers arrive two hours before a flight's arrival or departure to set up their tables and brew coffee. He makes sure he walks around and talks with the troops when they come through for processing. "I'm a combat veteran; the soldiers know I can relate to them," Peters says. "I tell them, 'It's OK to be scared. You stay scared, you stay alive.'" Peters also talks to the soldiers about the Adopt-A-Soldier program, asking them to fill out a card so a family can "adopt" them and send care packages and necessities to them in Iraq or Afghanistan.  Watch Peters and volunteers interacting with U.S. soldiers before their deployment to Iraq » . Peters says the most important thing is to show the soldiers "the support and the spirit that they need behind them as they step up to get on that plane." "Sometimes it breaks your heart because you ask yourself, 'Which one of these beautiful people is not coming home?'" But as long as there are soldiers deploying and returning, Peters says he'll be there.  Watch Peters talk about one of the highlights of his military career » . "I see the roots of our country and our future in every one of these soldiers," he says.

**SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN) —** Retired Vietnam veteran Walt Peters understands the fear of heading into combat, the experience of boarding a deployment flight and the relief of returning home safely.

For the past four years, Peters has regularly stood outside Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, offering encouragement to departing troops and welcoming back those returning from war. He is often one of the final people soldiers encounter before leaving and among the first to greet them when they come home. He sends deploying service members off with wishes of “Godspeed” and receives returning troops with pride and support.

Peters believes America owes its beauty and freedom to its military personnel and veterans. In his words, the soldiers themselves represent the nation’s freedom.

Now 64, Peters has greeted roughly 20,000 troops. Regardless of when a flight arrives or leaves—even when it is scheduled in the middle of the night—he is there to shake soldiers’ hands and present each of them with a small American flag. According to Peters, some of those flags have traveled to Iraq and returned. He views the gesture as giving troops a piece of their country while expressing gratitude for their service.

Other volunteers also attend each flight, but Peters carries out his work despite being almost completely blind. Nearly a decade ago, he learned that he had chemical diabetes after being exposed to Agent Orange during his tours in Vietnam. Although he has lost nearly all his vision in recent years, his commitment to supporting soldiers remains undiminished.

Peters says he never received this kind of appreciation when he deployed to Vietnam. No one told him they valued his service or thanked him for defending the country’s freedom. He is determined that today’s troops will board their planes knowing that an older Vietnam veteran cares about them.

His involvement began in 2004 through the Savannah Red Cross. A friend from his fraternal Moose Lodge invited him to help welcome a returning flight. Since then, Peters has become a leader among the flight greeters, recruiting and training volunteers of his own. His team includes fellow Moose members as well as Vietnam veterans.

There are too many military flights for Peters to attend every one, though he has covered as many as three flights within a 26-hour span. Peters and his team arrive two hours before each scheduled departure or arrival so they can arrange tables and prepare coffee. As troops go through processing, he circulates among them and starts conversations.

Because he is a combat veteran, Peters believes the soldiers recognize that he understands what they are experiencing. He reassures them that fear is natural and advises them that remaining alert and afraid can help keep them alive.

He also introduces troops to the Adopt-A-Soldier program. Peters encourages them to complete a card that allows a family to “adopt” them and mail care packages and essential supplies while they are stationed in Iraq or Afghanistan.

For Peters, the central purpose of the effort is to ensure that soldiers feel the encouragement and morale of those supporting them as they prepare to board their flights. At the same time, the experience can be painful. Seeing the troops leave sometimes makes him wonder which of them may never return.

Still, Peters intends to continue for as long as service members are departing for war and coming home. He says that in every soldier, he sees both the foundations of the United States and its future.

# Nearly blind Vietnam veteran stands watch for soldiers leaving home — and welcomes them back

**Savannah, Georgia** — At Hunter Army Airfield, goodbyes and homecomings often unfold under harsh lights and at inconvenient hours.

Soldiers shoulder heavy packs. Families cling to one another for a few final moments. Returning troops scan the crowd for familiar faces.

And near the terminal, there is often another familiar presence: Walt Peters.

Peters, a Vietnam veteran who is nearly blind, comes to the Savannah airfield to greet soldiers as they deploy and to welcome them when they return. His failing eyesight makes it difficult to see their faces, but it has not stopped him from showing up.

He listens instead — to the cadence of boots, the rumble of buses and the swell of voices when families realize their loved ones are finally home.

For Peters, the simple act of being there carries the weight of history. Many Vietnam veterans returned to a country deeply divided over the war, often without the public embrace later generations of service members would receive. Peters cannot change that past, but he can help ensure today’s soldiers do not leave or return unnoticed.

At deployment ceremonies, his presence offers a quiet message: Someone remembers what it is like to go.

At homecomings, the message is even simpler: Welcome back.

Hunter Army Airfield, part of the military community surrounding Savannah, regularly serves as a departure and arrival point for troops. The scenes can be emotional — parents comforting children, spouses holding back tears, soldiers trying to remain composed as they say goodbye.

Peters stands among them not as a relative or official, but as a fellow veteran.

His eyesight may limit what he can make out across a crowded terminal, yet those around him recognize his consistency. He does not need to see every uniform clearly to understand what the moment means.

There is no grand ceremony centered on him. The attention belongs to the soldiers and their families. Peters’ role is quieter: a handshake, a few encouraging words, a steady figure waiting near the doorway.

In a place defined by movement, he remains constant.

Each departure connects one generation of military service to another. Each return gives Peters a chance to offer the welcome that many veterans of his era felt they never received.

And so, as troops continue to pass through Hunter Army Airfield — leaving Savannah for missions far away or stepping back onto Georgia soil — Walt Peters keeps coming.

Nearly blind, he may not always see the soldiers clearly.

But he makes sure they know they have been seen.

He presses one into each service member’s hand, offering a few quiet words before they depart. When they return—tired, relieved, sometimes changed in ways no one can yet see—he comes back to welcome them home.

He cannot undo what happened to his generation, but he can make sure today’s troops experience something different. Each flag is both a gesture of gratitude and a promise: *You will not be forgotten. Someone will be waiting when you come back.*

He does not ask whether the wars are right or wrong. His commitment is to the people sent to fight them. In every handshake and homecoming, he gives younger service members the recognition many Vietnam veterans never received.

And so he keeps showing up—flag by flag, flight by flight—turning his own painful history into an act of care.

# Still Standing Watch: A Vietnam Veteran’s Mission to Welcome a New Generation Home

Long after his own war ended, the Vietnam veteran found another way to serve.

Retired now and living with severe vision loss caused by chemical-related diabetes, he can no longer clearly see the faces of the young soldiers gathering before deployment. But he knows their voices, their footsteps and the uneasy silence that settles over people preparing to leave home for war.

And he knows fear.

“It’s OK to be scared,” he tells them. “You stay scared, you stay alive.”

Over the years, the veteran has greeted roughly 20,000 soldiers—shaking hands, offering encouragement and giving deploying troops the kind of farewell he and many others of his generation never received.

His eyesight may have faded, but his sense of duty has not.

For many Vietnam veterans, returning home meant stepping into a nation divided over the war. There were few ceremonies, little public gratitude and scant understanding of what they had endured. That experience stayed with him. Rather than allow the hurt to harden into bitterness, he turned it into a promise: Today’s service members would know that someone was waiting for them, standing beside them and honoring their sacrifice.

At deployment gatherings, his message is direct. He does not pretend that courage means being fearless. He tells soldiers that fear can sharpen the senses, encourage caution and remind them of what they want to come home to.

His words carry the weight of experience. They come from someone who has lived through combat and then faced another battle years later as chemical diabetes took most of his sight. Tasks once done without thought became difficult. Faces blurred. Independence narrowed.

Still, he kept showing up.

That perseverance is part of what makes his presence so powerful. Soldiers see a man who has paid a lasting price for his service, yet continues to serve others. Families see someone who understands the mixture of pride and worry that accompanies every deployment. Fellow veterans see proof that purpose does not end with retirement—or with disability.

Greeting 20,000 soldiers is not a single heroic act. It is thousands of small ones: arriving, waiting, listening, extending a hand and repeating words of reassurance to one service member at a time.

His mission is simple, but its meaning is profound. He cannot change where the soldiers are going or remove the dangers ahead. What he can do is make sure they do not leave feeling unnoticed.

And when they return, he can help give them the homecoming his generation deserved.

The veteran’s world may now be shadowed by limited sight, but his example remains clear. Service is not always measured by rank, uniform or physical ability. Sometimes it is measured by the willingness to stand watch for others—again and again—so they know they are not alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

## Volunteers provide coffee, flags and comfort to deploying troops at Hunter Army Airfield

**HUNTER ARMY AIRFIELD, Georgia** — Before dawn, as soldiers prepare to leave for combat deployments, Walt Peters and a group of fellow volunteers are often waiting with fresh coffee, American flags and words of encouragement.

Their work is simple but deeply personal: make sure service members know they are supported before they depart—and welcomed home when they return.

At Hunter Army Airfield, the volunteers brew coffee, distribute flags and help promote Adopt-A-Soldier, an initiative connecting troops with people who can send letters, care packages and other reminders of home. They also offer something less tangible but equally important: a listening ear.

Deployment ceremonies can bring a mix of pride, anxiety and sadness. Returning troops may face their own emotional challenges as they reconnect with family members and adjust to life away from combat. Peters and the other volunteers try to provide a steady, reassuring presence through both transitions.

Sometimes that means handing a soldier a cup of coffee during a long wait. Other times, it means talking quietly with a service member or family member who is struggling with the uncertainty of separation.

The flags serve as visible symbols of community support. Volunteers place them in soldiers’ hands as they leave and wave them again when military aircraft return, turning arrivals and departures into moments of public recognition.

Through Adopt-A-Soldier, the group also encourages civilians to maintain that support throughout a deployment. Letters and packages can help bridge the distance between troops overseas and the communities awaiting their return.

For Peters and his fellow volunteers, the effort is not about ceremony or recognition. It is about showing up consistently—before missions begin, after they end and during the difficult moments in between.
